cards.body: Track everything you do for three days in 15-minute blocks — no judgment, just data. Almost everyone discovers their 'busy' days were 60% meetings, messages, and refills. You can't manage what you can't see, and memory lies.
cards.title: Do a time audit before anything else

cards.body: We consistently underestimate how long tasks take and overestimate what a day holds — the planning fallacy. Fix: multiply your gut estimate by 1.5. If it still fits, great; if not, you've just saved your evening.
cards.title: The planning fallacy is stealing your evenings

cards.body:
Hours are fungible; energy isn't. Schedule hard thinking for your sharp hours and admin for your slump. Two focused hours at your peak beat four foggy ones at midnight.
Protect the peak: that's the whole game.
Manage energy, not just hours. Sleep, movement, and real breaks are productivity tools, not rewards — skipping them borrows tomorrow's focus at loan-shark interest.

cards.explain: Memory edits the story — the log doesn't. The audit reveals where time actually goes before you try to redirect it.
cards.q: What reveals where your time REALLY goes?

questions.explain: The planning fallacy is systematic underestimation. The 1.5x multiplier absorbs the optimism tax.
questions.q: A task feels like 2 hours. Safer plan?

choices: 60% went to meetings, messages, and small stuff
questions.explain: That's the classic audit result — 'busy' was mostly reactive. The fix starts with seeing it.
questions.q: Typical result of a first time audit?

choices: Sharp hours for hard thinking, slump hours for admin
questions.explain: Match task difficulty to energy level. Peak hours are scarce — spend them on the work that matters.
questions.q: How should you schedule around energy?

choices: They're tools — skipping them borrows tomorrow's focus
questions.explain: Sleep and breaks aren't luxuries; they're inputs. Skimping charges brutal interest on tomorrow.
Three ordinary days in 15-minute blocks is enough to expose the patterns. Longer audits die of boredom.
questions.q: How long should a time audit run?

flashcards.back: Three days logged in 15-minute blocks — reveals where time actually goes.
Underestimating task time and overestimating the day. Counter: multiply estimates by 1.5.
Hard thinking in sharp hours, admin in the slump. Two peak hours beat four foggy ones.
Protect them for the hardest work — that's the whole game.

cards.body: Give every task a home on the calendar — a start and an end. 'Work on report 9:00–10:30' beats 'work on report today' because the box forces scope decisions. What doesn't fit the box gets renegotiated, not wished away.
cards.title: Timeboxing: appointments with your tasks

cards.body: If it takes under two minutes, do it now. Replying, filing, confirming — these tasks cost more to track than to finish. The rule clears the small stuff before it becomes a second to-do list.
cards.title: The 2-minute rule kills task clutter

cards.body:
Multitasking is rapid task-switching, and every switch charges a refocus tax — up to 25 minutes for deep work. One thing at a time isn't slow; it's the fastest way through.
Single-task, then switch deliberately.
Batch the small stuff: answer all messages twice a day instead of all day. Context-switching is the tax; batching is the loophole.

choices: Up to 25 minutes for deep work
cards.explain: Refocus is expensive. That's why 'quick checks' between tasks destroy deep work — each one recharges the tax.
cards.q: Roughly how much focus does one task-switch cost?

choices: A calendar block with a start and end time
questions.explain: The box forces scope decisions and protects the time. Intentions evaporate; appointments stick.

choices: Do it now — tracking costs more than doing
Add it to a list to do later
questions.explain: Under two minutes, the overhead of tracking exceeds the work. Clear it immediately.
questions.q: A task takes 90 seconds. 2-minute rule says…

choices: Rapid task-switching with a refocus tax each time
Doing two things truly at once
questions.explain: The brain switches, it doesn't parallelize — and every switch bills you refocus time.
Batching pays the switching tax once instead of fifty times. Urgent stuff still gets handled — just in groups.
questions.q: Best way to handle small messages?

choices: It forces scope decisions and protects focus
It makes the day feel shorter
questions.explain: The box is a commitment device: scope gets decided upfront, and the time is defended against everything else.

flashcards.back: A task gets a calendar block with start and end — forces scope decisions.
Under two minutes? Do it now — tracking costs more than doing.
Up to 25 minutes for deep work. Batch small tasks to pay it once.
Grouping similar small tasks together to pay the switching cost once.

cards.body: Draw the grid: urgent/not-urgent × important/not-important. Do the urgent-important now, schedule the important-not-urgent (that's where goals live), delegate or drop the rest. Most people drown in quadrant 3 — urgent but unimportant.
cards.title: The Eisenhower matrix sorts your chaos

cards.body: Every yes is a no to something else. 'I can't take that on this week' is a complete sentence — no apology tour needed. Boundaries aren't rude; they're how your priorities survive contact with other people's priorities.
cards.title: Saying no is a scheduling skill

cards.body:
Once a week, 20 minutes: what got done, what slipped, what's next. The review turns a to-do list into a system — without it, priorities rot and the same tasks haunt you for months.
Friday afternoon is the classic slot: close the week deliberately.
Quadrant 2 (important, not urgent) is where exercise, learning, and relationships live. If it's never scheduled, it never happens — urgency will always outshout importance.

cards.explain: Important-not-urgent is where goals live, and it never becomes urgent on its own. Schedule it or lose it.

questions.explain: Do quadrant 1 first — fires first. Then protect quadrant 2 before new fires start.
questions.q: Which quadrant do you handle first?

choices: 'I can't take that on this week' — no apology tour
questions.explain: A clean no protects your priorities. Over-explaining invites negotiation; brevity closes it.
questions.q: Best way to decline extra work?

choices: It turns a list into a system — priorities stop rotting
questions.explain: The review catches slipped priorities and resets the week. Without it, the same tasks haunt you for months.
Quadrant 2 holds everything important that never screams — it only happens if scheduled.
Urgent-but-unimportant is other people's priorities wearing a costume. Delegate it, or let it go.

flashcards.back: Urgent/important grid: do Q1, schedule Q2, delegate/drop Q3, ignore Q4.
Quadrant 2: important, not urgent — goals live here. Schedule it or lose it.
20 minutes weekly: what got done, what slipped, what's next. Turns a list into a system.
